notes:
I found enough for notes on every verse. They draw mostly on older commentaries (Calvin, Gill, Matthew Henry, Wesley/Benson, Ellicott, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown), plus David Guzik's Enduring Word and Bible Hub's study notes. I didn't get to read anything from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic or Orthodox sites, Lutheran sources, or anything on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are left out.

---

## Introduction (whole chapter)

- **Who Moab was:** Calvin says Isaiah is speaking against a nation who were neighbors to the Jews and related to them by blood; for we know that the Moabites were descended from Lot, who was Abraham's nephew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **Why the tone is sad:** Guzik points out that David of Israel had a Moabite great-grandmother named Ruth, and when David was fleeing from Saul, the king of Moab protected his parents. He thinks this history gives Isaiah a tone of empathy even while he announces judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-15/
- **Chapters 15–16 belong together:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) treats the two chapters as one prophecy and notes that Jeremiah has introduced much of this prophecy into his forty-eighth chapter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **Who the prophecy was for:** Calvin says the Moabites never heard it. Isaiah wrote for believers, so they would see God's providence behind the rise and fall of nations rather than chance. A second aim was to show the Jews that God cared about their safety. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **Background history:** Ellicott draws on 2 Kings 3 and the Moabite Stone. He notes that Dibon, Medeba, Nebo and Horonaim, all named in these chapters, also appear on the Moabite Stone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm

## v. 1

- **"Burden":** The Hebrew word (*massa*) often signifies a weighty message of doom or judgment. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/15.htm. Gill and Barnes both mention that the Targum (the ancient Aramaic paraphrase) calls it "the burden of the cup of cursing" for Moab to drink. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **"In a night":** Calvin takes this to mean a sudden, unexpected disaster. He thinks it also rebukes the Moabites for feeling safe behind their defences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm. Barnes agrees the phrase denotes the suddenness with which the calamity would come upon them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **An unusual reading:** Gill reports that some have thought this circumstance is mentioned with a view to the night work, that work of darkness of Lot and his daughter, which gave rise to Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **Ar and Kir:** Ellicott says both names mean "city." He identifies Kir with Kerak, which he calls probably the strongest Moabite fortress. He also notes that Mesha boasted of taking Nebo by a night attack. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/15-1.htm. Calvin notes Kir literally means "wall," but he takes both words as place names. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **Lesson drawn:** Calvin applies the verse to the ungodly in general: destruction comes on them when they expect nothing of the kind (1 Thess. 5:2–3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm

## v. 2

- **Going up to the temple:** Guzik pictures a Moabite man fleeing the destruction of his city, running to his temple and his pagan gods for protection and mourning. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Isa/Isa_15.cfm. Calvin sees a condemnation of the worship of Chemosh: the Moabites turn to their god but find no help. Worse, this only stirs up God's anger further. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **Translation question:** The KJV reads "Bajith" as a place name. JFB prefers "to the temple" and links it to the "sanctuary" in 16:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **Shaved heads and beards:** Calvin explains that Eastern peoples showed mourning by shaving head and beard, while Western peoples let them grow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm. JFB calls cutting off the beard the greatest mark of sorrow and mortification. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm

## v. 3

- **Mourning everywhere:** Guzik says the invasion brings great distress and mourning in Moab. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Isa/Isa_15.cfm
- **Why so much detail:** Calvin thinks Isaiah describes the mourning vividly so the Jews would almost see it happen. Moab was at peace at the time, so believers needed help to take the prophecy seriously. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm

## v. 4

- **Former Israelite towns:** Guzik quotes Wolf: these cities north of the Arnon once belonged to the tribe of Reuben, and Moab had gradually pushed Israel out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-15/
- **Even soldiers cry out:** Matthew Henry comments: See how easily God can dispirit the stoutest of men. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_15.cfm. Calvin says even the bold will mourn, and each person will be so taken up with his own grief that he won't think of his neighbour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm

## v. 5

- **Whose heart cries out?** Writers disagree here, though not along denominational lines.
  - *Matthew Henry (English Presbyterian):* this is real compassion. Moabites are enemies but also our fellow creatures, and the same cup could soon be ours. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_15.cfm
  - *Calvin (Reformed):* the prophets often take on the role of the people whose disaster they foretell, as if on a stage, to make a stronger impression. He also grants that the prophets shuddered at God's judgments even on the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
  - *Guzik (Enduring Word):* reads it as empathy rooted in the family ties through Ruth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-15/
- **Zoar:** Guzik notes the link with Lot, who fled to Zoar from Sodom before the incest in the mountain cave (Gen. 19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-15/. A footnote on the Calvin page cites the Jewish commentator Rashi (Jarchi): some would flee to Zoar as Lot, their father, once did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **"Three-year-old heifer":** This phrase is in older translations (KJV), not in the BSB. Calvin applies it to Zoar, a town never attacked and full of vigour. He would also accept applying it to the whole luxurious nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm

## v. 6

- Guzik: Moab's plains were fine grazing land, but under God's judgment the grass withers. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Isa/Isa_15.cfm
- Calvin admits the language is exaggerated but says it is still true: a land without God's blessing becomes like a desert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- Matthew Henry: famine is usually the sad effect of war. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm

## v. 7

- Guzik sees fleeing refugees, carrying with them all their possessions. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Isa/Isa_15.cfm
- Calvin: the people have nowhere safe to store their goods and must hide them among the willows. He mentions another view, that the brook is where the enemy divides the plunder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- Matthew Henry: people eager to pile up wealth rarely consider how quickly it can be taken away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm

## v. 8

- Guzik: Moab's pain is visible to all, and everyone around its borders sees God's judgment. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Isa/Isa_15.cfm
- Calvin: the disaster reaches from one end of the land to the other. The repeated "wailing" shows extreme grief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- Coffman on Beer-elim: This word literally means, `the well of the princes'; and it is perhaps the same as that mentioned in Numbers 21:14-18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-15.html

## v. 9

- **Dimon:** JFB says Dimon is the same town as Dibon (v. 2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm. A footnote on the Calvin page cites Rosenmüller: the name is a wordplay meaning "Bloodtown." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **"More upon Dimon":** Calvin says God will multiply the killing. He insists God is not cruel, even though the Assyrians were; God is justly punishing Moab's cruelty toward the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
- **The lion:**
  - Guzik: anyone who survives the night attack meets lions, because God will finish His work of judgment! https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Isa/Isa_15.cfm
  - Calvin: lions and wild beasts devour those who escape. The point is that the wicked cannot escape God's hand, and this is meant to comfort the godly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm
  - A footnote on the same page links the lions to the plague of lions in 2 Kings 17:25. The text was cut off before I could see who wrote it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/15.htm

---

## Where Protestant writers differ

The sources I read don't split along denominational lines on the meaning of any verse. The real debate is about **when the prophecy was fulfilled**:

- **Gill (Baptist):** probably Nebuchadnezzar's destruction (as in Jer. 48), though he lists others who say Shalmaneser or Sennacherib. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **Benson (Methodist), quoting Bishop Lowth (Anglican):** given in Hezekiah's first year and fulfilled in his fourth, when Shalmaneser probably marched through Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/15-1.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** begun by the Assyrian, and finished by the Babylonian emperors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/15-1.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Moab would be badly damaged but not quite ruined, for we find another prophecy of its ruin (Jer. 48), fulfilled by Nebuchadnezzar. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_15.cfm

The only other difference is how to read the prophet's grief in v. 5 (see above).

## Other views

- **Historical questions:** Bible Hub's study page asks why Moab is said to be destroyed "in a night" when there is no historical or archaeological record of such an event. Its answer is that Moab was paying tribute to Assyria by 701 BC and that many of these sites are now uninhabited mounds. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/15.htm. Coffman says every commentator mentions how hard the prophecy is to interpret, though the overall picture is clear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-15.html
- **Catholic and Greek translations of v. 1:** The Catholic Public Domain Version translates Kir as "the wall of Moab," and so does Brenton's English translation of the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint). https://biblehub.com/isaiah/15-1.htm. I found no Catholic or Orthodox commentary on the chapter itself.
